key_results: Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1: multirate processing adds decimators and expanders to ordinary DSP primitives so computation, transmission rate, and storage can be reduced without merely throwing information away.

Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1.1: in a two-band QMF coder, the average rate is one half the sum of the low- and high-band word lengths; assigning more bits to the perceptually or statistically important band yields compression.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1.3: a two-channel analysis/synthesis bank has the form Xhat(z)=T(z)X(z)+alias terms; perfect reconstruction requires all alias terms to vanish and T(z)=c z^-K.
Chapter 1, Secs. 1.1.2-1.1.4: polyphase decomposition is the structural mechanism that lets M-channel filtering run near the decimated rates rather than redundantly at the input rate.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.1: a z-transform expression alone does not uniquely specify a sequence; its region of convergence is essential, and the DTFT exists when the unit circle lies in that region.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.2: complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: input a^n produces H(a)a^n whenever the relevant transforms converge.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.2: a discrete LTI system is causal exactly when h(n)=0 for n<0 and BIBO-stable exactly when h is absolutely summable; a causal rational system is stable exactly when every pole is inside the unit circle.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.3: the minimum number of delays needed to realize a scalar rational transfer function equals its order; real filters can be implemented as real first- and second-order cascade sections.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.1.4: uniform sampling replicates the analog spectrum every 2pi/T; a signal limited to |Omega|<sigma can be recovered at sampling rate at least 2sigma, while certain bandpass signals admit lower rates under nonoverlap constraints.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.2: for a MIMO LTI system, a vector exponential v a^n is mapped to H(a)v a^n; causality and stability reduce to the corresponding property of every scalar matrix entry.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.2: the McMillan degree of a rational transfer matrix is the smallest number of delays among all its realizations, generalizing scalar filter order.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3.3: paraconjugation H~(z)=H*(1/z*) analytically extends conjugation on the unit circle; for matrices it also transposes, and H~H continues |H|^2 away from the unit circle.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3.3: paraconjugation replaces each zero by its reciprocal conjugate and exchanges minimum- and maximum-phase factors.

Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4.2: the four real FIR linear-phase types arise from symmetry versus antisymmetry and even versus odd order; the type determines forced zeros at omega=0 and/or pi, while coefficient pairing nearly halves multipliers.

Chapter 2, Secs. 2.4.2-2.4.3: a generalized-Hermitian rational function has linear phase on the unit circle; analytic continuation lets unit-circle equalities be treated as rational identities, and a causal stable rational linear-phase filter must be FIR.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.1: truncating the ideal sinc response gives a least-squares approximation, but increasing length narrows the Gibbs ripples without reducing their peak; a better window trades sidelobe height against mainlobe width.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.1: the Kaiser window exposes a practical two-parameter design: beta is selected mainly by desired attenuation and order N mainly by transition width.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.2: the discrete prolate sequence minimizes out-of-band energy under unit norm and is the principal eigenvector of a real symmetric positive-definite Toeplitz matrix; the optimum is unique and symmetric.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.3: the optimal lowpass eigenfilter is the unit-norm eigenvector associated with the smallest eigenvalue of a weighted positive-definite matrix R assembled from passband and stopband errors.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.4: Parks-McClellan/Remez design produces the minimum-order real linear-phase FIR response for a prescribed minimax equiripple specification, including unequal passband and stopband weights.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.5: a nonnegative zero-phase FIR response factors as H(z)=H0~(z)H0(z); choosing one zero from each reciprocal-conjugate pair produces the minimum-phase factor, unique up to a unit-magnitude constant.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.2.5: spectral factorization can yield a nonlinear-phase FIR filter of roughly half the zero-phase order, but the intermediate squared-magnitude design may need about twice the requested attenuation and can be numerically delicate.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.1: the bilinear map s=(1-z^-1)/(1+z^-1) maps the stable analog half-plane to the inside of the unit circle and relates analog and digital frequencies by Omega=tan(omega/2), requiring edge prewarping.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.2: an Nth-order Butterworth magnitude-squared response is maximally flat through derivative order 2N-1 at zero frequency and rolls off asymptotically at 20N dB per decade.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.3.3: elliptic filters are minimax among rational filters with prescribed orders and band edges; equiripple error in both bands can reduce order dramatically compared with Butterworth or linear-phase FIR designs.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.1: H is allpass with gain c exactly when H~(z)H(z)=c^2; poles and zeros occur in reciprocal-conjugate pairs, a stable causal allpass preserves signal energy up to c^2, and its impulse autocorrelation is c^2 delta(n).
Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.1: an Nth-order stable causal allpass has monotonically decreasing unwrapped phase with total change 2pi N around the unit circle.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.4.3: repeatedly extracting a reflection coefficient reduces a stable unit allpass to a lattice; |k_m|<1 at every stage is equivalent to stability, so quantization that preserves those bounds also preserves stability and the allpass property.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.6.1: a suitable real bounded power-complementary pair with symmetric/antisymmetric numerators is the half-sum and half-difference of two stable unit allpass functions whose orders add to the original order.

Chapter 3, Sec. 3.6.2: odd-order Butterworth, Chebyshev, and elliptic filters meet the allpass-decomposition conditions; their interlaced pole subsets make two-output implementations possible with roughly N multipliers total.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.1: expansion by L compresses the spectrum and creates L images, whereas decimation by M stretches and sums M shifted spectra; spectral overlap in that sum is aliasing.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.1: the standard L/M converter expands by L, lowpass-filters, then decimates by M; the common filter both removes interpolation images and prevents decimation aliasing.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.1.2: a uniform DFT analysis bank can be generated from one prototype H0(z) by Hk(z)=H0(zW^k); the delay-chain/DFT interpretation connects filter banks to sliding short-time Fourier analysis.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.2: an L-fold expander and M-fold decimator commute exactly when L and M are relatively prime.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.2: the noble identities move a rational filter G(z^M) across an M-fold rate changer, converting high-rate filtering into the equivalent low-rate operation.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3: every H(z) has Type 1 polyphase form H(z)=sum_{l=0}^{M-1} z^-l E_l(z^M); Type 2 contains the same components in a different cyclic ordering.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.1: an M-fold polyphase decimator performs filtering after downsampling and saves approximately a factor M in arithmetic; the dual interpolator avoids all multiplies on inserted zeros.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.2: an M-channel DFT bank needs only the prototype's polyphase subfilters plus one M-point DFT rather than M separate full-rate filters.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.3: when L and M are coprime, the fractional converter can be rearranged so every polyphase computation occurs at the lower internal rate; its arithmetic per output is essentially independent of L.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.3.5: multirate systems are generally linear periodically time-varying, but alias cancellation can make an overall analysis/synthesis system LTI; a simple DFT-bank construction reconstructs a scaled delayed input exactly.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.4.1: IFIR realizes a narrowband filter as G(z^M1) followed by an image suppressor I(z); stretching reduces model-filter order while the suppressor removes the newly created passband images.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.4.2: a large rate change should often be factored into stages so early filters operate at favorable rates and later filters see relaxed transition specifications; the best factorization balances per-stage orders and rates.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.1: H is Nyquist(M) when one polyphase component is a monomial, equivalently its impulse response has periodic zero crossings and its M uniformly shifted frequency responses sum to a constant.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.1: a real zero-phase FIR half-band lowpass has equal passband/stopband ripple, band edges symmetric about pi/2, and an impulse-response length constrained to 4J+3 in the nontrivial case.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.2: power complementarity means sum_k |Hk(e^jomega)|^2=c and supports exact reconstruction with paraconjugate synthesis filters; an FIR complementary mate can be obtained by spectral-factorizing 1-|H0|^2.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.2: relatively prime FIR analysis filters are Euclidean complementary, so Bezout synthesis polynomials exist for causal FIR exact reconstruction, although poor scaling can make the construction numerically impractical.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.3: the M polyphase components of H(z) are power complementary if and only if G(z)=H~(z)H(z) is Nyquist(M).

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.6.5: adjustable multilevel filters are weighted sums of M shifted versions of one Nyquist(M) prototype; the Nyquist shifted-sum property prevents bumps and dips between independently tunable band levels.

Chapter 4, Secs. 4.7.2-4.7.3: for y_{k+1}=Py_k+q with P=I-alpha A, residual and error obey r_k=P^k r_0 and e_k=P^k e_0; stalling is domination by the eigenmode whose eigenvalue has the largest magnitude.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4.7.4: when the iteration operator behaves like a lowpass filter, high-frequency residual modes die first and the stalled residual is smooth enough to decimate to a coarser grid.

Chapter 4, Sec. 4.7.4: multigrid solves a smaller coarse-grid error equation, interpolates that error to the fine grid, and corrects the stalled estimate; the coarse operator is chosen as A^(2Delta)=M_D A^(Delta) M_I.

For the two-channel analysis/decimation/synthesis bank, the reconstructed spectrum separates into a desired term and an aliased term: X-hat(z)=T(z)X(z)+A(z)X(-z). The X(-z) component is created by decimation and expansion, not by the filters alone. [§5.1.1, Eqs. 5.1.4–5.1.6, Figs. 5.1-1–5.1-3]

The standard two-channel alias-cancellation choice F0(z)=H1(-z), F1(z)=-H0(-z) makes A(z)=0. A QMF bank is generally linear periodically time varying with period two; alias cancellation reduces the input–output relation to LTI filtering by T(z). [§5.1.1, Eqs. 5.1.7–5.1.10, Fig. 5.1-4]

Amplitude distortion means |T(e^{jω})| is not constant; phase distortion means arg T(e^{jω}) is not linear. Perfect reconstruction requires T(z)=cz^{-n0}, so the output is only a scaled and delayed input. [§5.1.2, Eqs. 5.1.11–5.1.15]

Under the simple QMF relation H1(z)=H0(-z), polyphase decomposition gives T(z)=2z^{-1}E0(z²)E1(z²). For causal FIR H0, this constraint cannot produce a useful exact-PR selective bank; the PR solution collapses to a sum of two delays. [§§5.2–5.2.1, Eqs. 5.2.1–5.2.8]

An FIR prototype H0 can eliminate phase distortion when it has odd order and linear phase, leaving only amplitude distortion. The residual ripple originates where adjacent lowpass/highpass responses overlap, so prototype design balances stopband attenuation against flatness of their squared-magnitude sum. [§5.2.2, Eqs. 5.2.9–5.2.15, Fig. 5.2-3]

Using stable allpass polyphase components makes |T(e^{jω})| exactly constant, eliminating amplitude distortion at low arithmetic cost, but generally leaves nonlinear phase. [§5.2.3, Eqs. 5.2.16–5.2.19, Fig. 5.2-5]

A power-symmetric lowpass obeys H0(z)H-tilde0(z)+H0(-z)H-tilde0(-z)=β. For a real, stable, bounded-real, odd-order, power-symmetric transfer function with numerator symmetry, Theorem 5.3.1 yields a decomposition into two real stable allpass polyphase components. [§§5.3–5.3.2, Theorem 5.3.1, Eqs. 5.3.1–5.3.15]

Odd-order power-symmetric elliptic filters have poles on the imaginary axis in the analog prototype, and the passband/stopband specifications are coupled by δ2²=4δ1(1−δ1) and ωp+ωs=π. [§§5.3.3–5.3.4, Eqs. 5.3.16–5.3.22]
The IIR power-symmetric QMF implementation exploits allpass sections and needs only (N−1)/4 multiplications and (N+1)/2 additions per input sample for odd prototype order N. [§5.3.5, Table 5.10.2]

A nonnegative zero-phase halfband filter can be spectrally factored to obtain an FIR power-symmetric H0; with mirrored/time-reversed companions, all four filters have equal odd order and the bank is exact PR. [§5.3.6, Eqs. 5.3.23–5.3.30, Table 5.10.3]

An M-channel maximally decimated bank reconstructs the original component plus M−1 frequency-shifted alias components. The alias-component matrix compactly maps those M spectral copies to the output. [§§5.4.1–5.4.3, Eqs. 5.4.3–5.4.9]

With analysis and synthesis polyphase matrices E(z) and R(z), the end-to-end polyphase product is P(z)=R(z)E(z). A common exact-PR condition is R(z)E(z)=cz^{-m}I, which makes every polyphase branch a common delay and scale. [§§5.5–5.6, Eqs. 5.5.8–5.6.4]
The delay-chain filter bank provides the canonical trivial PR construction: it splits a signal into its M polyphase subsequences and interleaves them back exactly. [§5.6.1, Fig. 5.6-2]

Theorem 5.7.1 states that an M-channel maximally decimated bank is alias-free if and only if P(z)=R(z)E(z) is pseudocirculant. Perfect reconstruction is the special pseudocirculant case with only a delayed monomial in the desired component. [§5.7.2, Theorem 5.7.1, Figs. 5.7-2–5.7-3]

Tree-structured banks recursively split selected subbands, producing uniform or nonuniform channel partitions while reusing two-channel building blocks; PR is inherited when the constituent stages are PR. [§5.8, Figs. 5.8-1–5.8-4]

A transmultiplexer is the dual arrangement that combines independent inputs into one signal and later separates them. The same polyphase machinery connects crosstalk cancellation in a transmultiplexer to alias cancellation in a filter bank. [§§5.9.1–5.9.2, Figs. 5.9-1–5.9-4]

A causal stable p×r transfer matrix H(z) is lossless when H†(e^{jω})H(e^{jω})=dI on the unit circle; for rational systems this is the paraunitary identity H-tilde(z)H(z)=dI, and necessarily p≥r. [§6.1.1, Eqs. 6.1.1–6.1.4]

For a square paraunitary matrix, the paraconjugate provides the inverse up to scale. Its determinant is allpass; in the causal FIR case the determinant is a scaled delay. Its columns are mutually orthogonal power-complementary vector filters. [§6.1.1, Eqs. 6.1.5–6.1.8]

Cascades, substitutions H(z^M), transposition, and unitary coordinate rotations preserve paraunitariness. Givens rotations and diagonal delay matrices therefore serve as elementary lossless building blocks. [§6.1.2, Figs. 6.1-1–6.1-6]

If the FIR analysis polyphase matrix E(z) is paraunitary, choosing R(z)=cz^{-K}E-tilde(z) gives PR. For IIR E(z), this direct paraconjugate synthesis is generally unstable, which motivates the chapter’s FIR restriction. [§6.2.1, Eqs. 6.2.1–6.2.4]

Paraunitary analysis makes each synthesis filter a scaled time-reversed conjugate of its analysis counterpart, fk(n)=c h*k(L−n); analysis and synthesis filters consequently have identical lengths and magnitude responses. [§6.2.1, Eqs. 6.2.6–6.2.9]

Theorem 6.2.1: any two of these properties imply the third—E(z) is lossless, synthesis filters are time-reversed conjugates of analysis filters, and the bank has perfect reconstruction. [§6.2.1, Theorem 6.2.1]

A paraunitary E(z) makes the analysis filters power complementary; the alias-component matrix is paraunitary exactly when E(z) is; and each product Hk(z)H-tilde_k(z) is an Mth-band (Nyquist(M)) filter. [§6.2.2, Eqs. 6.2.10–6.2.18]

For causal real two-channel FIR banks, Theorem 6.3.1 links equivalent descriptions: power symmetry of H0, the odd-delay mirror relation for H1, paraunitariness of E(z), and paraunitariness of the alias-component matrix. [§6.3.1, Theorem 6.3.1]

The two-channel paraunitary QMF lattice remains PR under arbitrary coefficient quantization because each normalized lattice section remains unitary/paraunitary. Lattice coefficients can be recovered recursively from a valid impulse response by order reduction. [§§6.4.1–6.4.2, Figs. 6.4-1–6.4-3]

Direct lattice design optimizes angular or reflection parameters for stopband rejection while PR remains automatic throughout the search; it avoids the numerically delicate spectral-factorization route. [§6.4.3, Fig. 6.4-4]

The QMF lattice combines low complexity, structural PR, power symmetry, robustness to coefficient quantization, and a hierarchical property: deleting terminal sections gives a lower-order bank that is still PR. [§§6.4.4–6.4.5]

A general M-channel FIR paraunitary polyphase matrix of degree J factors into elementary degree-one sections V_m(z)=I−v_mv_m†+z^{-1}v_mv_m† and a constant unitary matrix, permitting unconstrained optimization over unit vectors and unitary factors. [§5.6.3; §§6.5.1–6.5.2, Eqs. 6.5.1–6.5.4, Table 6.7.1]

In transform coding, an orthogonal transform decorrelates block samples; for a wide-sense stationary source, the KLT formed from autocorrelation eigenvectors gives the optimal energy-compaction basis under the chapter’s assumptions. Independent blocking, however, creates visible or audible block-boundary artifacts. [§6.6.1]

The lapped orthogonal transform overlaps neighboring length-2M windows while retaining M transform outputs per block. It is a paraunitary filter-bank subclass that reduces blocking artifacts without abandoning critical sampling or PR. [§6.6.2, Eqs. 6.6.1–6.6.8, Fig. 6.6-2]

Paraunitariness is sufficient but not necessary for FIR perfect reconstruction; the chapter’s Venn diagram organizes general alias-free banks, PR banks, FIR PR banks, and paraunitary subclasses by progressively stronger matrix and determinant conditions. [§6.7.1, Fig. 6.7-1]
A ‘linear-phase filter bank’ means that each analysis filter has linear phase; it is distinct from merely having a linear-phase distortion function T(z). [§7.0]

A nontrivial two-channel FIR exact-PR bank cannot simultaneously keep every analysis filter linear phase, retain power complementarity/paraunitariness, and impose H1(z)=H0(-z). Linear phase plus power complementarity forces each filter to degenerate to a sum of two delays. [§7.1, Eqs. 7.1.1–7.1.5]

The Chapter 7 lattice propagates an image-pair of polynomials P(z),Q(z) through elementary sections so that H0 remains symmetric and H1 antisymmetric; its inverse supplies synthesis filters and exact reconstruction. [§7.2, Eqs. 7.2.2–7.2.8, Figs. 7.2-1–7.2-2]
Lemma 7.3.1 supplies the order-reduction step behind formal synthesis of the linear-phase PR lattice for the stated broad class, apart from mild exceptional cases. [§7.3, Lemma 7.3.1]

A cosine-modulated bank generates M real analysis filters from one real lowpass prototype by pairing conjugate frequency shifts among 2M complex modulations. The prototype cutoff is approximately π/(2M). [§8.1.1, Eqs. 8.1.1–8.1.7, Figs. 8.1-1–8.1-4]

The pseudo-QMF construction cancels the important adjacent-channel aliases exactly while treating distant-channel leakage as negligible when prototype stopband attenuation is high. Choosing fk(n)=hk(N−n) makes the distortion function linear phase, although the individual analysis filters are generally not linear phase. [§§8.1.2–8.1.4, Eqs. 8.1.17–8.1.38, Fig. 8.1-5]

For a linear-phase prototype, |T(e^{jω})| has period π/M. Its amplitude ripple is concentrated in transition regions where two neighboring modulated responses overlap, so flattening the sum of their squared responses controls the entire bank’s amplitude distortion. [§8.2.1, Eqs. 8.2.1–8.2.7, Fig. 8.2-1]

Pseudo-QMF prototype design minimizes a weighted combination of distortion-function nonflatness φ1 and prototype stopband energy φ2. The tradeoff parameter selects between reconstruction ripple and subband rejection. [§8.2.2, Eqs. 8.2.8–8.2.9]

Polyphase implementation computes the 2M prototype components first and then applies one M×2M cosine-modulation matrix; noble identities move the decimators left so the component filters operate at the lowest rate. Ignoring fixed modulation overhead, analysis costs about N/M multiplications and additions per input sample. [§8.3, Eqs. 8.3.1–8.3.8, Figs. 8.3-1–8.3-2]

The relevant type-IV DCT and DST matrices are real, symmetric, orthonormal, and related by row signs and column reversal. Consequently C²=S²=I and both transforms are self-inverse. [§8.4.1, Eqs. 8.4.1–8.4.7, Fig. 8.4-1]

When the prototype length obeys N+1=2mM, the two halves of the cosine-modulation matrix can be written in terms of DCT/DST matrices and diagonal sign matrices, enabling fast-transform analysis and synthesis structures. [§8.4.2, Eqs. 8.4.8–8.4.25]

Theorem 8.5.1: for a real symmetric prototype of length N+1=2mM, the cosine-modulated analysis polyphase matrix E(z) is paraunitary if and only if each pair Gk(z),G_{M+k}(z) of its 2M prototype polyphase components is power complementary. [§8.5.1, Theorem 8.5.1, Eqs. 8.5.1–8.5.10]

Each power-complementary polyphase pair can be parameterized by a two-channel lossless lattice. Optimizing the lattice angles is therefore unconstrained: every iterate remains paraunitary, so perfect reconstruction is preserved automatically while only prototype stopband energy must be minimized. [§8.5.2, Figs. 8.5-1–8.5-2]

Prototype symmetry cuts the independent lattice count approximately in half; the cosine-modulated PR design has about mM/2≈N/4 free parameters, roughly half the pseudo-QMF count. Increasing m adds one section to every lattice and gives a hierarchical initialization strategy. [§8.5.2, Eqs. 8.5.11–8.5.15, Fig. 8.5-3]

For both pseudo-QMF and cosine-modulated PR banks, polyphase implementation requires approximately (N+1)/M MPUs and N/M APUs plus modulation cost. Cosine-modulated PR is substantially cheaper than a general M-channel paraunitary cascade for the same N and M. [§8.5.3, Tables 8.5.1–8.5.4]

The cosine modulation itself can be implemented with fast DCT/DST algorithms when N+1=2mM. Analysis and synthesis share the same order, synthesis filters are time reversals of analysis filters, and the bank retains exact PR at the price of a modest prototype stopband-attenuation loss. [§§8.5.4–8.5.5, Figs. 8.5-5–8.5-6]

§9.2.1, Eqs. (9.2.2)-(9.2.3), book pp. 397-398: under the standard roundoff model, quantizer error is taken as zero-mean, white, WSS, uniformly distributed over one step, and mutually uncorrelated across quantizers and with the input; the text explicitly warns that deterministic inputs can violate this model.

§9.2.2, Eqs. (9.2.4)-(9.2.5), book pp. 399-400: a quantizer's contribution to output-noise variance equals its source variance multiplied by the energy of its noise transfer function; uncorrelated contributions add in variance.
§9.2.2, book p. 400: increasing fixed-point word length by one bit quarters the quantization-noise variance, an improvement of 6.02 dB.

§9.2.3, book pp. 400-404: scaling can prevent overflow but reduces signal-to-roundoff-noise ratio when internal quantizer noise is unchanged; sum scaling is sufficient for bounded inputs, while L2 scaling is appropriate for finite-energy or WSS analyses.

§9.3, book pp. 405-406: decimation preserves WSS mean and variance and maps autocorrelation as Ryy(k)=Rxx(Mk), whereas expansion generally destroys WSS because output variance becomes periodic in time.
Theorem 9.3.1, book pp. 407-408: if x(n) is white, mutually uncorrelated, zero-mean, and equal-variance (WUZE) and T(z)T~(z)=dI, then y(n)=T(z)x(n) is WUZE with variance multiplied by d.

§9.5.2 and Table 9.5.1, book pp. 413-416: paraunitary structure makes the complete QMF bank's output roundoff noise white and yields simple structure-dependent variance formulas; the M-channel cascaded FIR PR case gains roughly 6.02 dB over the comparable direct two-channel cases when M=2.

§9.6, Eqs. (9.6.3)-(9.6.6), book pp. 416-418: a stable first-order feedback section with |a|<1 and a passive quantizer satisfying |Q(x)|<=|x| cannot sustain zero-input granular or overflow limit cycles; the state magnitude must fall by at least one quantization step until it reaches zero.

§9.7.1, Eq. (9.7.1), book pp. 419-420: in a structurally passive realization whose magnitude cannot exceed unity for any admissible coefficient values, a nominal unity passband extremum can only move downward under coefficient perturbation, so its first-order sensitivity to every coefficient is zero.

§9.7.2, book pp. 421-423: allpass-based power-symmetric IIR QMF banks and FIR PR-QMF lattices retain their bounded/power-complementary structure after admissible multiplier quantization, giving much lower passband sensitivity than direct-form realizations.

Theorem 10.1.1, book pp. 430-432: the M-by-M blocked version of a scalar H(z) is pseudocirculant, its first row is formed from H's Type-1 polyphase components, and it is paraunitary exactly when the scalar filter is allpass.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.2: the normal rank of a polynomial matrix is its maximum rank over the z-plane; a square matrix has full normal rank exactly when its determinant is not identically zero.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.2: a polynomial matrix is unimodular exactly when its determinant is a nonzero constant, equivalently when its inverse is also polynomial.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.2, Facts 13.2.1-13.2.2: unimodular right factors preserve left coprimeness, and every zero of det P(z) produces a pole in at least one entry of P^-1(z).

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.3: the McMillan degree of a causal rational transfer matrix is the minimum number of delay elements in any realization and need not equal the largest power appearing in its matrix entries.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.1, Eqs. 13.4.10-13.4.13: a realization (A,B,C,D) has transfer matrix H(z)=D+C(zI-A)^-1B and impulse response h(0)=D, h(n)=CA^(n-1)B for n>0.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.1: every pole of H(z) is an eigenvalue of A; the converse is guaranteed only for a minimal realization because unreachable or unobservable modes can cancel.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.1: similarity transformation maps (A,B,C,D) to (T^-1AT,T^-1B,CT,D), changing state coordinates but preserving the input-output system and eigenvalues.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.2, Lemmas 13.4.1 and 13.4.3: reachability is equivalent to full row rank of [B AB ... A^(N-1)B], while observability is equivalent to full column rank of the vertically stacked [C; CA; ...; CA^(N-1)].
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.2, Eq. 13.4.31: the observability matrix times the reachability matrix is a block Hankel matrix of impulse-response samples h(1) through h(2N-1).
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.2, Theorem 13.4.1: a realization is minimal if and only if it is both completely reachable and completely observable.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.2, Lemma 13.4.6: any two minimal realizations of the same transfer matrix have equal dimension and are related by a unique similarity transformation.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.2, Theorem 13.4.2: the PBH test detects unobservable right eigenvectors annihilated by C and unreachable left eigenvectors annihilated by B.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.4.3, Lemma 13.4.8: for observable (C,A), existence of P>0 satisfying A†PA+C†C=P implies A is stable; conversely stable A yields a unique positive-definite solution given by the convergent observability-Gramian sum.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.5.1, Theorem 13.5.1: finite polynomial elementary operations reduce any polynomial matrix to a unique Smith form whose monic diagonal invariant factors divide their successors.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.5.2, Lemma 13.5.1: a greatest left common divisor R satisfies the matrix Bezout relation QVq+PVp=R; left-coprime Q and P therefore satisfy QVq+PVp=I.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.5.2, Corollaries 13.5.2-13.5.3: irreducible MFDs for the same system differ by a unimodular left factor, and det Q is invariant up to nonzero scale with minimal possible polynomial order.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.5.3, Theorem 13.5.2: every rational transfer matrix has a Smith-McMillan form with relatively prime numerator/denominator invariants obeying nested divisibility; these invariants are unique up to scale.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.6, Theorem 13.6.1: for an irreducible MFD and minimal realization, a pole is equivalently a zero of det Q, a zero of the leading Smith-McMillan denominator invariant, and an eigenvalue of A; away from zero it also generates a persistent exponential output from some FIR input.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.7, Theorem 13.7.1: for full-normal-column-rank systems, a transmission zero of order K is exactly a point at which an input with a Kth-order pole can produce an FIR output.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.7: unlike the scalar case, a MIMO transfer matrix can possess a pole and transmission zero at the same z-plane location without cancellation.

Chapter 13, Sec. 13.8, Theorem 13.8.1: McMillan degree equals the sum of the orders of the Smith-McMillan denominator invariants, equals the order of det Q for any irreducible MFD, and equals the dimension of any reachable-observable realization.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.8: for a square transfer matrix, degree(det H) can be smaller than but never exceeds the McMillan degree of H.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.9, Lemma 13.9.1: a minimal FIR realization has a nilpotent A with A^N=0; conversely A^N=0 guarantees an FIR transfer matrix.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.10.1: a square causal system has a causal inverse exactly when its direct term h(0)=D is nonsingular; the inverse realization uses A-BD^-1C and has the same McMillan degree.
Chapter 13, Sec. 13.10.2: causal unimodular means precisely causal FIR with a causal FIR inverse; both the original and inverse state matrices are nilpotent.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.2: a p-by-r causal system is lossless when it is stable and H~(z)H(z)=c^2I; this requires p>=r, and for square systems the inverse is H~/c^2.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.2.1: losslessness is equivalent to preserving every finite-energy input's energy up to c^2, and its impulse response satisfies sum_n h†(n)h(n+k)=c^2I delta(k).
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.2.1: for square lossless H, det H is stable allpass; in the FIR case it is a scaled pure delay.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.3, Theorems 14.3.1-14.3.2: every real 2x2 or 2x1 FIR lossless system admits a complete minimal lattice of Givens rotations and unit delays; arbitrary angle choices preserve losslessness.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.4.1: V(z)=I-vv†+z^-1vv† for unit-norm v is a normalized-lossless degree-one system with det V=z^-1 and V(1)=I.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.4.2, Theorem 14.4.1: every degree-N MxM FIR lossless matrix factors into N degree-one diadic blocks followed by a constant unitary matrix, yielding an N-delay minimal realization.

Chapter 14, Secs. 14.4.3-14.4.4: every degree-N Mx1 FIR lossless vector has the analogous minimal factorization; unlike the square case, each minimal diadic factor is unique up to an irrelevant unit-magnitude phase.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.5, Eq. 14.5.9: a unitary realization matrix gives an instantaneous conservation law: increase in state energy equals input energy minus output energy.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.5.1, Theorem 14.5.1: a causal stable transfer matrix is normalized lossless exactly when it has some state-space realization whose constant realization matrix [A B; C D] is normalized unitary.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.5.2: for square H, stable A plus a unitary realization matrix implies the realization is both observable and reachable, hence minimal.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.6.1: any real normalized MxM unitary matrix factors into M(M-1)/2 planar Givens rotations plus fixed signs, matching its real degrees of freedom.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.6.2: any complex unitary matrix factors into M-1 Householder reflections and a diagonal phase matrix; the normalized complex family has M^2 real degrees of freedom, while the real family has M(M-1)/2.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.7: the Smith-McMillan invariants of a square FIR lossless system are causal pure delays z^-n_i with n0>=...>=n_(M-1)>=0 and sum n_i equal to system degree.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.7, Theorem 14.7.1: every pole p of a square causal lossless system is paired with a zero 1/p*, all zeros lie outside the unit circle, and degree H equals degree det H; the determinant contains every system pole and zero.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.8: a normalized square lossless matrix satisfies H†(z)H(z)<=I outside the unit circle and >=I inside; equality in a direction means the system is memoryless in that direction.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.9.1: replacing z^-1 in the FIR diadic block by any stable first-order allpass section gives a degree-one IIR lossless block, and every degree-N square IIR lossless system factors into N such blocks plus a constant unitary matrix.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.9.2: an Mx1 IIR lossless vector can be stripped of its nonzero poles one at a time, leaving an FIR lossless remainder; complex-conjugate pole stages can be paired to obtain real structures.

Chapter 14, Sec. 14.10.1: all FIR or IIR lossless cascades can be rewritten as Householder matrices separated by diagonal one-coordinate allpass sections, saving one addition per stage while retaining minimality.
Chapter 14, Sec. 14.11.1: direct coefficient quantization of Givens factors generally destroys equal column norms and thus unitarity for M>2; two dimensions are a special exception.

Chapter 14, Secs. 14.11.1-14.11.2: norm-compensated Householder and diadic blocks remain scaled-unitary/lossless for arbitrary nonzero quantized vectors, allowing paraunitarity and filter-bank perfect reconstruction to survive coefficient quantization.

Appendix A, Secs. A.6-A.8: normal matrices are exactly those unitarily diagonalizable; every square matrix is nevertheless unitarily triangularizable, and Rayleigh extrema of a Hermitian quadratic form are its smallest and largest eigenvalues.
Appendix B, Sec. B.2: a zero-mean WSS white process has autocorrelation sigma^2 delta(k) and flat PSD sigma^2; nonzero mean adds a spectral impulse at DC.

Appendix B, Sec. B.3: stable LTI filtering multiplies a WSS input PSD by |H|^2; white-noise output variance is sigma_x^2 times the impulse-response energy, and variances from uncorrelated sources add.
Appendix B, Sec. B.5: a vector WSS process passed through H has Syy=H Sxx H†; a blocked scalar WSS process has a Toeplitz zero-lag covariance matrix.
Appendix C, Sec. C.1: under the high-resolution uniform-noise model, quantizer error variance has the form c·2^-2b sigma_x^2, making precision, signal variance, and overflow margin inseparable.
Appendix C, Sec. C.2.1: at fixed average rate, ideal subband quantization noise is minimized by equalizing all subband quantizer-noise variances—equivalently, align the least-significant bits.

Appendix C, Sec. C.2.2: ideal subband coding gain is the arithmetic-to-geometric mean ratio of subband variances, is never below one under the model, and approaches the reciprocal spectral-flatness measure as M grows.
Appendix C, Sec. C.2.2: GSBC(M) need not be monotone in M, but GSBC(nM)>=GSBC(M) for positive integer n and no finite-band value exceeds the asymptotic gain.

Appendix C, Secs. C.3.2-C.3.3: the KLT diagonalizes the input autocorrelation matrix and maximizes transform-coding gain; the optimum gain is the AM/GM ratio of its eigenvalues and is nondecreasing with block size.
Appendix C, Secs. C.3.3-C.5.2: ideal SBC, asymptotic KLT, infinite-order DPCM prediction gain, and the Gaussian rate-distortion bound share the same dependence on spectral flatness.

Appendix C, Sec. C.4.1: ideal SBC decorrelates distinct subband processes at all time offsets for any WSS input, whereas the KLT decorrelates same-time transform coefficients and must be retuned when input statistics change.

Appendix C, Sec. C.4.2: for a finite-degree paraunitary coder, optimality requires both minimizing the determinant of the output covariance and diagonalizing it; the general constrained solution is identified as an open problem.

Appendix D, Sec. D.1.1: the complex cepstrum of a causal minimum-phase factor is causal, while outside-unit-circle zeros produce an anticausal component; folding that component is the key to minimum-phase factor recovery.
Appendix D, Sec. D.1.2: cepstral computation must use consistently unwrapped phase and remove the integer-delay phase ramp; the unwrapped phase change from -pi to pi reveals that delay.
Appendix D, Sec. D.2, Eqs. D.2.2-D.2.3: a causal stable minimum-phase sequence with positive first sample can be reconstructed recursively from its causal cepstrum.

Appendix D, Sec. D.3: a nonnegative zero-phase FIR response can be minimum-phase spectral-factorized without root finding—even with unit-circle zeros—by radial scaling, complex cepstrum computation, anticausal folding, and cepstral inversion.
Appendix E, Eq. E.4: Mason's formula gives a flow graph transfer function as the sum of each forward-path gain times the determinant of its path-deleted graph, divided by the full graph determinant.
pedagogy: A mathematically mature, theorem-and-construction treatment that develops multirate DSP by repeatedly moving among exact input-output equations, spectra, polyphase matrices, state-space descriptions, and realizable structures. The book opens with engineering motivation and concise signals/filter reviews, then builds its core in a deliberate sequence: maximally decimated banks, perfect reconstruction, paraunitary and linear-phase designs, cosine modulation, finite-wordlength behavior, block/LPTV formulations, time-frequency and wavelet systems, multidimensional lattices, and finally MIMO/lossless foundations. Proofs are substantial and frequently constructive: noble identities and alias equations are derived rather than asserted; degree-reduction, spectral-factorization, and lattice arguments end in implementations; impossibility results and counterexamples identify incompatible constraints; and numerical designs compare filter order, attenuation, delay, MPUs/APUs, coding gain, and sensitivity. Equivalent representations are the principal teaching device—QMF versus polyphase matrix, block filtering versus LPTV system, STFT or wavelet transform versus filter bank, lattice geometry versus multidimensional sampling, and frequency-dependent paraunitarity versus a constant unitary realization matrix. Intuition comes from canonical spectra, commutators, pole-zero diagrams, geometric lattice pictures, worked specifications, and carefully chosen engineering applications, but the algebra carries the argument. Prerequisites grow from discrete-time signals, DTFT/z-transform, FIR/IIR design, and complex matrices to optimization, random processes, state space, advanced linear algebra, lattices, and vector Fourier methods; the review chapters and appendices provide compact just-in-time foundations rather than an introductory treatment. At least 307 assigned exercises appear across Chapters 2-14 and Appendices A, C, D, and E. They range from spectral sketches and arithmetic counts to theorem proofs, matrix identities, filter-bank/lattice synthesis, finite-precision analysis, multidimensional designs, coding-gain derivations, and transfer-function extraction; several deliberately complete proofs or algorithms only outlined in the prose. Summary tables at major transitions make the work usable as both a rigorous advanced course text and a long-lived reference. Because the official source is scan-derived, headings and prose are searchable, while equations intended for publication should be verified against the page image.

gems: Chapter 1's oversampled audio example makes the analog/digital bargain concrete: sample at twice the eventual rate behind a gentler analog anti-alias filter, perform a sharp linear-phase digital filter, then decimate.

The historical audio rates—48 kHz studio, 44.1 kHz compact disc, and 32 kHz broadcast—turn abstract rational rate conversion into the demanding 48-to-44.1 kHz interface later revisited as L=441, M=480.
The extreme QMF bit-allocation thought experiment assigns all bits to the lowpass channel when the input is overwhelmingly lowpass, making perceptual/statistical compression visible in one equation.
The text treats an M-channel filter bank as a generalization of a short-block Fourier analyzer, a compact conceptual bridge between filter-bank spectra and transform methods.
The paraconjugate notation looks cosmetic at first, then becomes the language that unifies magnitude squares, reciprocal-conjugate zeros, allpass filters, and power complementarity.

A zero-phase ideal lowpass truncated to greater length gets a narrower transition but stubbornly retains roughly the same Gibbs peak—an excellent corrective to the intuition that more taps fix every error.
Design Example 3.2.1 turns omega_p=0.2pi, omega_s=0.3pi, and 40 dB attenuation into a Kaiser beta of about 3.395 and order about 46, clearly separating the roles of attenuation and transition width.
The prolate sequence and eigenfilter are dual-looking eigenproblems: maximize in-band window energy with the largest eigenvalue, but minimize filter approximation error with the smallest eigenvalue.

For one specification, the book contrasts elliptic order 7, Butterworth order 28, and linear-phase equiripple FIR order 101; the cost advantage is dramatic, but the elliptic group delay varies roughly from 10 to 60 samples.

A 7th-order elliptic pair implemented through two allpass branches needs 7 multipliers and 22 adders versus 11 and 14 in a direct implementation, showing why multiply count alone does not decide the best structure.
The rational 3/2 rate-converter example needs only about an 11th-order linear-phase filter for its stated 0.01 ripple, and polyphase symmetry reduces this to six multipliers.

A 32-channel, order-50 DFT bank falls from roughly 1,632 multiplications in direct filtering to 187 using polyphase-plus-DFT structure; after decimation, the prototype filtering costs only about six real multiplications per input interval.

The simple DFT filter bank formed from delay chains is exactly perfect-reconstruction despite its crude roughly 13 dB channel selectivity: it returns M^2 x(n-M+1), separating reconstruction algebra from subband quality.
In the IFIR example, a direct order-233 linear-phase filter using 117 multipliers is replaced by a stretched order-131 model plus order-6 image suppressor using 70 multipliers.

The 50-fold 8 kHz-to-160 Hz decimator drops from an estimated order 2028 and about 21 million multiplies/s to a multistage design with orders 90 and 139 and about 3.72 million multiplies/s—roughly a sixfold saving.
A subband-coding example compresses a 10 ksample/s, 16-bit stream from 160 kb/s to 120 kb/s simply by splitting into two critically decimated bands and assigning 16 versus 8 bits.
The voice-privacy system is almost mischievously simple: split speech into bands, permute them in frequency and optionally in time, then invert the permutation for authorized recovery.

Euclidean complementarity promises causal FIR exact reconstruction from relatively prime analysis filters, then immediately warns that the unique low-degree synthesis pair can be oppositely selective and so poorly scaled that quantization overwhelms the reconstruction constant.

The woofer/tweeter crossover example distinguishes allpass complementarity from power complementarity: an undistorted sum does not by itself guarantee that the second branch is a good highpass, so doubly complementary filters solve two different engineering requirements.
The phrase polyphase is explained physically: each decimated phase approximates a fractional phase ramp e^(j omega l/M), and the M nearly equal-magnitude terms align in the prototype passband.

Multigrid appears in a signal-processing text because a stalled residual is often smooth: stationary iteration behaves like lowpass filtering, so the stubborn error is precisely the part that can be represented cheaply on a coarser sampled grid.

Problem 4.30 packages an efficient half-band design trick: design a Type 2 one-band equiripple filter at half the final order, substitute z^2, add a delay, and obtain the alternating zeros and nonnegative response required later for perfect-reconstruction banks.

The Johnston 32D example makes ‘almost PR’ concrete: a length-32/order-31 linear-phase QMF with ωs=0.586π reaches at least 38 dB stopband attenuation and only ±0.025 dB peak amplitude distortion at 16 MPUs and 16 APUs. [§5.2.2, Fig. 5.2-4; Table 5.10.1]

The simplest alias-free QMF constraint produces a sharp impossibility result: demanding FIR exact reconstruction under H1(z)=H0(−z) leaves no useful selective solution—only two delayed taps. [§5.2.1, Eqs. 5.2.7–5.2.8]

Power-symmetric elliptic design turns a special pole geometry into an exceptionally compact QMF: the odd-order analog prototype has imaginary-axis poles that separate cleanly into two real allpass branches. [§§5.3.3–5.3.5, Fig. 5.3-2]

The delay-chain bank is a useful zero-mystery baseline: before designing frequency-selective filters, one can see perfect reconstruction simply by deinterleaving and reinterleaving the M residue classes of the sample index. [§5.6.1, Fig. 5.6-2]

Alias-free M-channel reconstruction has a visually memorable exact criterion: the polyphase product must be pseudocirculant. PR is not a separate trick but the most concentrated member of that family. [§5.7.2, Theorem 5.7.1]

Tree-structured banks connect rigorous PR algebra to pyramid-style subband analysis: only selected leaves need be split, so resolution can follow the signal rather than a uniform frequency grid. [§5.8]
The filter-bank/transmultiplexer duality recasts the same algebraic error: alias leakage in one diagram becomes channel crosstalk when the diagram is turned around. [§5.9]

Quantizing every coefficient in the two-channel paraunitary lattice does not destroy perfect reconstruction, provided paired analysis/synthesis sections use the quantized values consistently; structural identities survive where direct-form coefficient cancellations may not. [§6.4.1]

The order-63 direct lattice example achieves roughly 74 dB stopband attenuation while avoiding the extreme intermediate attenuation and delicate spectral factorization that the halfband route would demand. [§6.4.3, Fig. 6.4-4]

The lattice is hierarchical in a particularly teachable sense: every truncated cascade is itself a lower-order PR filter bank, so increasing filter length does not require abandoning the previous valid design. [§6.4.5]

A complexity comparison exposes three different currencies: an order-21 FIR PR bank needs about 12 MPUs and 11 APUs with no phase distortion, while an order-5 IIR allpass bank needs about 1 MPU and 3 APUs but has a group-delay spread around 14 samples. [§6.7.2, Table 6.7.4]

The LOT is introduced as the cure for transform coding’s hard block boundaries: overlap neighboring blocks but keep exactly M coefficients per shift, obtaining smoother joins without giving up PR. [§6.6.2, Fig. 6.6-2]
Chapter 7 turns a design wish list into a tradeoff theorem: nontrivial FIR exact PR, per-filter linear phase, and paraunitarity/power complementarity cannot all be had simultaneously. [§7.1]

The linear-phase comparison is unusually candid: the order-63 PR lattice reaches 42.5 dB stopband rejection and exactly zero reconstruction error at 17 MPUs/49 APUs, whereas Johnston’s approximate design of the same order reaches about 65 dB and 0.002 dB residual amplitude distortion. [§7.2, Fig. 7.2-3 and Table 7.2.1]
A near-PR Johnston design can initialize the exact-PR linear-phase lattice by setting the even reflection coefficients to zero, converging much faster than a random start. [§7.2]

The eight-channel pseudo-QMF example uses a length-40/order-39 prototype; adjacent filters cross near −3 dB, alias terms remain small, and MT(z) is nearly a single delay with dominant coefficient 0.9988325. [§8.2.2, Tables 8.2.1–8.2.2, Figs. 8.2-2–8.2-5]

Theorem 8.5.1 reduces a large M-channel PR constraint to M independent two-function statements: pair each prototype polyphase component with the one M positions away and make the pair power complementary. [§8.5.1]

For M=17 and prototype order 101, cosine-modulated PR needs only eight three-angle lattices—24 optimized parameters—versus 51 for pseudo QMF and 216 for a general paraunitary design. [§8.5.2, Design Example 8.5.1; §8.5.3]

The same M=17, N=101 comparison quantifies the price of exactness: cosine-modulated PR gives 35.72 dB prototype stopband attenuation with reconstruction and alias errors near 10^-15, while pseudo-QMF variants reach about 38.4–40.7 dB but retain measurable errors. [§8.5.3, Table 8.5.3]

The chapter’s practical verdict is that exact cosine-modulated PR usually costs less than 5 dB of stopband attenuation relative to pseudo QMF, while using fewer design parameters and essentially the same implementation cost. [§§8.5.3–8.5.5]

Fast DCT implementation completes the progression from theorem to architecture: a shared prototype, paired lossless lattices, and one fast modulation transform realize a many-channel exact-PR bank without implementing M unrelated filters. [§§8.3, 8.4, 8.5.4]
A pole at a=0.99 gives a first-order noise gain of about 50, a sharp numerical reminder that stability alone does not imply benign finite-word behavior. [§9.2.2, Eq. (9.2.6), book p. 400]

One extra fractional bit buys almost exactly 6.02 dB less roundoff-noise variance; Table 9.5.1 then shows an architectural change that can buy the same improvement without adding a bit. [§§9.2.2 and 9.5.2, book pp. 400 and 415-416]

Passive quantization turns a nonlinear feedback argument into a finite countdown: every nonzero first-order state loses at least one step Delta per sample and must hit zero, excluding both granular and overflow limit cycles. [§9.6, book pp. 417-418]

The 6-bit allpass implementation and 8-bit order-23 QMF lattice retain strikingly cleaner passbands than direct-form versions at identical precision, making structural passivity visible rather than merely asserted. [§9.7.2, Figs. 9.7-2 and 9.7-3, book pp. 421-423]

Blocking a scalar filter by M permits an input sample rate M times faster than one computational unit can handle, paid for by M-way parallel hardware; the exact same diagram is an alias-free maximally decimated bank. [§10.1.1, book pp. 428-430]

The first-difference sampler stores 16-bit even samples and 8-bit differences, reducing a slowly varying signal from 16 to an average 12 bits per original sample while retaining exact FIR reconstruction. [§10.2.1, Fig. 10.2-7, book pp. 441-442]

For arbitrary order M, the alternating-binomial difference matrix is its own inverse, so a seemingly exotic sampling theorem reduces to synthesis filters no longer than M. [§10.2.1, Eqs. (10.2.14)-(10.2.20), book pp. 442-444]

The two-of-three nonuniform sampling design reconstructs a length-71 approximately bandlimited sequence with an order-72 lowpass (stopband attenuation above 55 dB) and an order-50 Hilbert transformer. [Design Example 10.2.1, Fig. 10.2-16, book pp. 449-451]

The STFT's best finite symmetric window for concentrating energy in a chosen band is the prolate spheroidal sequence, tying a practical window-design question back to the eigenfilter construction. [§11.2.1, book pp. 468-469]
A Gaussian is not just a customary STFT window: it is the unique waveform that reaches the RMS uncertainty bound Dt*Df=0.5. [§11.2.4 and Problem 11.6, book pp. 477-478 and 540-541]

Design Example 11.4.1 reuses one 23rd-order power-symmetric FIR pair to make both a four-channel equal-band generalized STFT and a three-level octave wavelet bank, with orthonormal bases in both cases. [§11.4.2, Figs. 11.4-2 and 11.4-3, book pp. 506-508]

Replacing z by z^3 in the Haar filters preserves paraunitariness but destroys continuous-time wavelet orthogonality; the counterexample pinpoints why the infinite-level Nyquist(1) condition is genuinely additional. [Example 11.5.6, Figs. 11.5-9 and 11.5-10, book pp. 525-529]

The maximum-regularity construction with K=L=3 starts from an order-10 maximally flat half-band filter and produces an order-5 spectral factor with three zeros at omega=pi. [Design Example 11.5.2, book pp. 535-536]

Packing circular spectra on a hexagonal reciprocal lattice uses six nearest neighbors instead of four and cuts the required sampling density by a factor of about 1.15. [§12.3.2, Figs. 12.3-1 through 12.3-3, book pp. 569-572]
For the support geometry in Fig. 12.4-2, rectangular decimation can reduce density only by two without aliasing, while hexagonal decimation can reduce it by four. [§12.4.1, book pp. 573-575]

The generalized DFT for the chapter's determinant-four hexagonal matrix happens to be exactly the ordinary 4-point DFT up to indexing, but the text immediately warns that this coincidence is not general. [Example 12.4.6, Eq. (12.4.43), book pp. 592-594]

Example 12.7.2 converts rectangular samples directly to a hexagonal lattice—without returning to analog—by interpolating horizontally and then applying a quincunx decimator at unchanged net density. [§12.7.2, Figs. 12.7-3 through 12.7-5, book pp. 612-615]

A quincunx 2D QMF bank inherited from Johnston's 32D one-dimensional prototype reaches a peak distortion of about 0.05 dB, exactly twice the corresponding 1D value. [Example 12.9.3, Fig. 12.9-10, book pp. 637-640]
Example 13.3.2 makes McMillan degree tangible: H(z)=z^-1R requires rank(R), not matrix size, delays because the rank factorization shares state across channels.
The nonminimal structure of Fig. 13.4-6 is a fine trap: both delays connect to input and output, yet x1(n)=x2(n)=u(n-1), so arbitrary states remain unreachable.
Equation 13.4.31 is described as a beautiful significance: multiplying the observability and reachability matrices literally lays out impulse-response blocks h(1) through h(2N-1).
The Smith-form worked example uses nothing fancier than polynomial long division and elementary row/column operations, yet produces invariants that control poles, zeros, degree, and coprimeness.

The text highlights a uniquely discrete-time advantage: unimodular polynomial pre/postfilters in z are realizable FIR systems, so a finite input can probe each Smith-McMillan invariant from outside the MIMO system.
A MIMO system can have a pole and zero at the same point without cancellation; a diagonal example makes the scalar intuition fail immediately.
Example 13.10.1 infers degree indirectly: a causal unimodular matrix appears first-order, its inverse visibly contains z^-2, and equal inverse degree proves both systems have degree two.

The Chapter 14 structures embody the author's design philosophy: constraints should live in interconnection topology so optimization parameters can vary independently without leaving the lossless family.
The degree-one block I-vv†+z^-1vv† has a memorable geometric meaning—delay exactly the component along v and pass the orthogonal complement untouched—while its determinant is exactly z^-1.

Even z^-1I requires M successive degree-one diadic extractions; highest FIR power stays unchanged until the last relevant direction is peeled away, vividly separating polynomial order from McMillan degree.
The realization matrix gives an instantaneous conservation law, not merely an integrated one: state-energy growth equals current input energy minus current output energy.
A frequency-dependent paraunitary condition for every omega is made equivalent to unitarity of one constant state-space matrix, a striking compression of an infinite family of constraints.
Householder factors are self-inverse reflections that turn arbitrary vectors into coordinate axes; the same geometry powers both unitary-matrix factorization and lossless filter structures.
Two-channel Givens lattices are a lucky finite-precision exception: after cosine/sine quantization their columns still have equal norms, whereas higher-dimensional cascades generally lose unitarity.
Appendix C's practical rule for optimum bit allocation is almost visual: align the least-significant bits across subbands so all quantizers have the same step size and noise variance.
A 6 dB coding gain is translated directly into one saved bit per sample, giving the AM/GM variance ratio an immediate communications meaning.
Example C.2.1 deliberately breaks an attractive intuition: a constructed spectrum gives GSBC(2) about 1.0256 but GSBC(3)=1, so more ideal bands can reduce coding gain.

The KLT and ideal subband coder arrive at the same asymptotic gain by different routes—one through Toeplitz covariance eigenvalues, the other through ever-narrower spectral bands—and DPCM reaches it through infinite-order prediction.

The finite-degree paraunitary coding-gain problem is left honestly unresolved: the system must both reduce the output-covariance determinant and diagonalize the result, a constrained generalization of the KLT.
The DPCM loop acts like a sophisticated quantizer: it quantizes the small prediction error with b bits yet reconstructs a larger signal with an effective precision greater than b.
Appendix D avoids root finding entirely and still handles unit-circle zeros; the recommended half-band settings are concrete—radial factor rho about 1.02 and FFT length about 8N.

Design Example D.3.1 factors an order-178 nonnegative half-band response: the original reaches about 80 dB stopband attenuation and its minimum-phase factor about 40 dB, exactly reflecting the magnitude-square relationship.
Mason's formula is taught by literally deleting each forward path and recomputing the leftover loop determinant, making a symbolic graph theorem operational rather than ceremonial.

The two-page list of important summaries is itself a useful navigation artifact: it identifies the book's canonical synthesis tables, culminating in three adjacent lossless-system tables on pages 772-774.
